category: Strings II: Characters, Encodings & Pattern Symbols
description: Character-level operations and encodings, additional string manipulation functions (padding, partitioning, rotation, extraction), case and character-class predicates, number-string conversions (IntegerString, RomanNumeral), transliteration, and the anchor and character-class symbols used in string patterns.

tools.name: ToCharacterCode
tools.description: Converts a string to a list of integer character codes (Unicode code points by default, or in a named encoding such as "UTF8" or "ISO8859-1"); FromCharacterCode is the inverse. Use them for byte-level protocols, checksums, Caesar-style ciphers and inspecting non-ASCII text.
tools.notes: For binary data prefer StringToByteArray / ByteArrayToString, which return ByteArray objects.

tools.name: StringToByteArray
tools.description: Encodes a string as a ByteArray in UTF-8 (or another encoding); ByteArrayToString decodes. These are the correct functions for hashing strings, writing binary streams, sockets and BaseEncode/Base64 work, since ByteArray is the type used by Hash, Encrypt, Export["Byte"] and network functions.
tools.example:
ba = StringToByteArray["héllo"];
Normal[ba] (* byte list *)
Hash[ba, "SHA256", "HexString"]
BaseEncode[ba] (* base64 *)

tools.name: $CharacterEncoding
tools.description: The default character encoding used for text I/O and external strings ("UTF-8" on modern systems); $SystemCharacterEncoding is the operating-system default. Import, Export, OpenRead etc. accept CharacterEncoding -> "enc" to override per operation; $CharacterEncodings lists the supported names.

tools.name: LetterQ
tools.description: Character-class predicates: LetterQ (all letters), DigitQ (all digits), UpperCaseQ, LowerCaseQ test whole strings; StringQ tests for a string. Use them for validation and as pattern tests (s_String?DigitQ).

parameters.name: string
parameters.description: String to test (True only if every character qualifies; empty string gives True for LetterQ/DigitQ).

tools.example:
DigitQ["12345"] (* True *)
LetterQ["abc1"] (* False *)
Select[tokens, UpperCaseQ]
tools.notes: For single-character classes inside patterns use LetterCharacter, DigitCharacter etc.

tools.name: Capitalize
tools.description: Capitalizes the first character of a string; Capitalize[s, "AllWords"] capitalizes every word and "TitleCase" applies title-case rules (minor words stay lower-case). Decapitalize lowers the first character. Language-aware and Unicode-safe, unlike ad-hoc ToUpperCase[StringTake[...]] code.

parameters.name: string
parameters.description: Input string or list of strings.

tools.example:
Capitalize["the lord of the rings", "TitleCase"] (* "The Lord of the Rings" *)
Decapitalize["Hello"] (* "hello" *)

tools.name: StringPadRight
tools.description: Pads a string on the right to length n with spaces or a given padding string (truncating if longer); StringPadLeft is its mirror (already listed). Use it for fixed-width text tables and aligned console output.

tools.name: StringPartition
tools.description: Splits a string into substrings of length n (with optional offset d for overlapping windows), the string analogue of Partition. Use it for fixed-width record parsing, chunking hex/base64 text and n-gram extraction.

tools.name: StringExtract
tools.description: Extracts the n-th whitespace-separated field of a string, or nested fields with custom delimiters (StringExtract[s, "delim1" -> i, "delim2" -> j]). It is a compact alternative to StringSplit + Part for parsing log lines and delimited records.
tools.usage:
StringExtract["string", n]
StringExtract["string", {n1, n2, ...}]
StringExtract["string", "delim" -> n]
StringExtract["string", "delim1" -> n1, "delim2" -> n2]

parameters.name: n
parameters.description: Field index (negative counts from the end; All for all fields).

parameters.name: delim
parameters.description: Delimiter string or pattern for each level.

tools.name: StringPart
tools.description: Gives the n-th character (or characters at several positions) of a string as a string; StringTakeDrop returns {taken, rest} like TakeDrop, and StringRotateLeft/StringRotateRight rotate characters cyclically. Small utilities that avoid Characters/StringJoin round trips.
tools.usage:
StringPart["string", n]
StringPart["string", {n1, n2, ...}]
StringTakeDrop["string", n]
StringRotateLeft["string", n]
StringRotateRight["string", n]

parameters.name: n
parameters.description: Position or count (negative from the end).

tools.name: StringReplacePart
tools.description: Replaces the characters between positions m and n (or several ranges) with a new string, working positionally rather than by pattern. Use it when edit positions come from StringPosition or fixed-width layouts.
tools.usage:
StringReplacePart["string", "new", {m, n}]
StringReplacePart["string", "new", {{m1, n1}, {m2, n2}, ...}]
StringReplacePart["string", {"new1", "new2"}, {{m1, n1}, {m2, n2}}]

tools.name: StringReplaceList
tools.description: Gives the list of all strings obtained by applying a replacement rule to a single match at a time (one result per match), instead of replacing every match at once as StringReplace does. Useful for enumerating single-edit variants and for rewriting-system experiments.
tools.usage:
StringReplaceList["string", patt -> rhs]
StringReplaceList["string", {rule1, rule2}, n]

tools.name: StringEndsQ
tools.description: Tests whether a string ends with a given string or string pattern (with operator form and IgnoreCase option), the counterpart of StringStartsQ. Use it for file-extension checks and suffix filtering.
tools.usage:
StringEndsQ["string", patt]
StringEndsQ[patt]["string"]
StringEndsQ["string", patt, IgnoreCase -> True]

tools.name: IntegerString
tools.description: Converts an integer to a string in base 2-36 (default 10), optionally zero-padded to a given length; also supports named forms such as "Roman", "Chinese", "Devanagari". It is the direct way to build fixed-width numeric labels, hex strings and file-name counters.
tools.usage:
IntegerString[n]
IntegerString[n, b]
IntegerString[n, b, len]
IntegerString[n, "Roman"]

parameters.name: b
parameters.description: Base 2-36 or a named numeral form.

parameters.name: len
parameters.description: Pad with leading zeros to this length.

tools.notes: FromDigits["ff", 16] parses back. BaseForm only formats for display.

tools.name: IntegerName
tools.description: Gives the English (or other language) name of an integer as words ("one thousand two hundred"), with forms such as "Ordinal", "Cardinal", "Words" and "Digits". Use it for cheque-style amounts, ordinals in generated text and localized output.
tools.example:
IntegerName[1234] (* "one thousand two hundred thirty-four" *)
IntegerName[3, "Ordinal"] (* "third" *)
IntegerName[42, "German"]

tools.name: RomanNumeral
tools.description: Converts an integer to a Roman numeral string; FromRomanNumeral parses one back to an integer. Handy for section numbering and date formatting.

tools.name: RemoveDiacritics
tools.description: Strips accents and other diacritical marks from letters (é -> e, ñ -> n); Transliterate converts text from any script to the Latin alphabet (or between scripts). Both are used for search normalisation, slug generation and matching names across data sources.

tools.name: CharacterName
tools.description: Gives the Unicode (or Wolfram long) name of a character, with FromCharacterCode/ToCharacterCode for codes; CharacterRange, LetterNumber and FromLetterNumber map letters to positions in an alphabet (optionally for a given language). Useful for text analysis and alphabet arithmetic.

tools.name: CharacterCounts
tools.description: Gives an association of each character (or n-gram of characters) in a string with its number of occurrences, sorted by count. Use it for frequency analysis, entropy estimates and classical cipher breaking.

tools.name: AlphabeticSort
tools.description: Sorts strings in true alphabetical order for a given language (ignoring case and diacritics appropriately), unlike Sort, which orders by character code; AlphabeticOrder compares two strings the same way. Use them for user-facing sorted lists of names.
tools.example:
AlphabeticSort[{"zebra", "Apple", "éclair", "banana"}] (* {"Apple", "banana", "éclair", "zebra"} *)
Sort[{"zebra", "Apple"}] (* {"Apple", "zebra"} by code point; lowercase would sort after uppercase *)

tools.name: PalindromeQ
tools.description: Tests whether a string or list reads the same backwards, ignoring case for strings. A small utility that also works on integers via IntegerReverse comparisons.

tools.name: InsertLinebreaks
tools.description: Inserts newline characters into a string so that no line exceeds n characters (default 78), breaking at whitespace. Use it to wrap long text for console output, comments and fixed-width exports.

tools.name: StringToStream
tools.description: Opens an input stream that reads from a string, so that Read, ReadList, ReadLine and ReadString can parse in-memory text exactly like a file. Use it to parse formatted text (numbers, words, records) without writing temporary files.
tools.usage:
stream = StringToStream["string"]
Read[stream, Number]
ReadList[stream, Word]
Close[stream]

tools.name: NumberString
tools.description: String pattern that matches the characters of a number (digits with optional sign, decimal point and exponent). Use it in StringCases to pull numeric values out of text, then ToExpression or Interpreter to convert.
tools.usage:
StringCases["string", NumberString]
StringCases["string", n : NumberString :> ToExpression[n]]
tools.notes: NumberString matches a broad numeric syntax; use DigitCharacter.. for plain integers.

tools.name: Whitespace
tools.description: Whitespace matches a sequence of one or more whitespace characters and WhitespaceCharacter a single one; with StringTrim, StringSplit and StringReplace they handle spacing normalisation. Related classes: PunctuationCharacter, HexadecimalCharacter, WordCharacter (alphanumeric), LetterCharacter, DigitCharacter.
tools.usage:
StringSplit["string", Whitespace]
StringReplace["string", Whitespace -> " "]
StringCases["string", WordCharacter ..]
StringDelete["string", PunctuationCharacter]
tools.example:
StringSplit["a  b\tc\nd", Whitespace] (* {"a", "b", "c", "d"} *)
StringCases["0x1F and 0xA0", "0x" ~~ HexadecimalCharacter ..]

tools.name: StartOfString
tools.description: Anchor symbols for string patterns: StartOfString / EndOfString match the string boundaries, StartOfLine / EndOfLine match line boundaries and WordBoundary matches between a word and non-word character. They correspond to the regex anchors ^, $ and \b and make StringReplace/StringCases precise.
tools.usage:
StringReplace[s, StartOfString ~~ Whitespace -> ""]
StringCases[s, StartOfLine ~~ "#" ~~ Except["\n"] .. ~~ EndOfLine]
StringCases[s, WordBoundary ~~ "cat" ~~ WordBoundary]
tools.example:
StringReplace["cat concatenate", WordBoundary ~~ "cat" ~~ WordBoundary -> "dog"] (* "dog concatenate" *)
StringCases["# title
text
# other", StartOfLine ~~ "# " ~~ t : Except["
"] .. :> t]

tools.name: OrderlessPatternSequence
tools.description: A pattern sequence that matches its elements in any order, usable in ordinary expression patterns and in SubsetCases-style matching. Use it to match argument lists whose order is irrelevant without enumerating permutations.

tools.name: IgnoreCase
tools.description: Option for StringMatchQ, StringCases, StringReplace, StringPosition, StringFreeQ, StringContainsQ, StringStartsQ/EndsQ, StringSplit and NotebookFind: IgnoreCase -> True makes matching case-insensitive without rewriting the pattern. RegularExpression["(?i)..."] is the regex alternative.
tools.usage:
StringCases[s, patt, IgnoreCase -> True]
StringReplace[s, "error" -> "E", IgnoreCase -> True]
StringMatchQ[s, "*.CSV", IgnoreCase -> True]
tools.example: StringContainsQ["Fatal ERROR occurred", "error", IgnoreCase -> True] (* True *)

tools.name: Overlaps
tools.description: The Overlaps option of StringCases, StringCount, StringPosition and SequenceCases controls whether overlapping matches are returned: False (default for most), True (all overlapping matches starting at different positions) or All (every match). Important when counting repeated motifs such as "aa" in "aaa".
tools.usage:
StringCases[s, patt, Overlaps -> True]
StringCount[s, patt, Overlaps -> True]
StringPosition[s, patt, Overlaps -> False]

tools.name: TemplateObject
tools.description: There is no StringFormat function; string formatting is done with StringTemplate ("`name`" or "`1`" slots, TemplateApply), StringForm ("`` and `1`" with ToString), NumberForm-family wrappers, or StringJoin/StringRiffle. TemplateObject, TemplateSlot, TemplateIf, TemplateSequence and TemplateExpression are the general template language used by StringTemplate, FileTemplate, XMLTemplate and NotebookTemplate.
tools.usage:
StringTemplate["Hello `name`, you are `age`"][<|"name" -> "Ann", "age" -> 30|>]
TemplateApply["`1` + `2` = `3`", {1, 2, 3}]
FileTemplate["report.html"][assoc]
TemplateObject[{"x = ", TemplateSlot["x"]}]
tools.example:
tpl = StringTemplate["<* TemplateIf[#ok, \"passed\", \"failed\"] *>: `n` tests"];
tpl[<|"ok" -> True, "n" -> 12|>]

tools.name: UpTo
tools.description: UpTo[n] in StringTake, Take, StringPartition and similar functions requests at most n elements without an error when fewer exist, replacing manual Min[Length, n] logic. Use it for safe truncation of user text and previews.
tools.usage:
StringTake[s, UpTo[n]]
Take[list, UpTo[n]]
StringSplit[s, " ", UpTo[k]]
tools.example:
StringTake["short", UpTo[10]] (* "short", no error *)
preview = StringTake[text, UpTo[80]] <> "..."
